messages.content: We have 45 minutes for family game night. How should we use it?
How many people are playing, and do you want one game or a little variety?
Four of us, including a seven-year-old. Variety sounds fun.
Try a five-minute setup, a 15-minute drawing game, and a 20-minute card game, leaving five minutes to wrap up. Pick games everyone already knows so explaining rules doesn't eat the evening.
We only have a deck of cards and paper.
That works. Start with quick drawing-and-guessing rounds, then play a familiar card game. If nobody agrees on a card game, keep drawing and let each person choose a prompt.
The seven-year-old might get upset about losing.
Make the drawing game cooperative: see how many prompts the group can guess together. For cards, choose a game with short rounds or play in pairs, and agree that anyone can switch back to drawing.
I have a box of keepsakes and don't know how to start sorting it.
What would make the result useful to you: finding things more easily, reducing the box, or simply getting a sense of what's inside?
Finding things. I'm not ready to throw anything away.
Start with broad groups such as photos, letters, and small objects. Keep an 'unsure' pile and put everything back afterward; nothing needs to be discarded.
Some things fit more than one group.
Choose the category where you'd first expect to look for each item. If that isn't clear, leave it in 'unsure' for now. A short note on the container can point to related items elsewhere.
I only have half an hour this weekend.
Use ten minutes to scan the contents, fifteen to make broad groups, and five to put them back with temporary labels. It's fine if you only sort part of the box.
What if looking through it feels overwhelming?
Stop or switch to a smaller handful. You could label the remaining contents 'unsorted' and return another day; organizing them doesn't require making emotional decisions on a deadline.
I want to learn pottery, but my schedule is unpredictable. What format should I pick?
Are you hoping mainly to try it once, build a regular practice, or make a particular object? Also, do you have access to a studio?
I want to see if I enjoy it. There's a studio nearby, but I don't know its schedule.

A single introductory session could give you a feel for the craft without committing to a series. A self-paced hand-building kit is another option, though the experience and finishing process may differ from a studio.
I can't reliably book anything more than a few days ahead.
A self-paced kit may fit that constraint better. Alternatively, check whether the studio offers short-notice openings; I don't know if it does. Compare any cancellation terms before booking.
I'm not keen on having clay mess at home.

That shifts the balance toward a studio session. Look for a drop-in or short-notice class, if available. If neither exists, waiting for a suitable opening may be easier than buying a kit you won't enjoy using.
The studio has a Saturday drop-in, but it fills up quickly.

You could treat it as a trial: decide on a Saturday when you're free, check availability, and have a backup activity in case it's full. Confirm whether the session includes materials and firing if those details matter to you.
If I like it, should I sign up for a six-week course?

Not necessarily right away. Ask about missed-class and cancellation options, then compare the commitment with another drop-in. A course makes sense if its schedule and terms fit your actual availability.
Where should we put a community notice board?
Who needs to see it, and what locations are you considering? It would also help to know who can approve installation at each site.
Residents should see it. We're considering the lobby or the outside wall, but nobody has approved either.

The lobby may protect notices from weather; the outside wall may reach people who don't enter the building. Both depend on the relevant owner's or manager's permission. You could compare visibility and accessibility first, then request approval for your preferred spot.
The lobby is narrow, and the outside wall gets rain.

A small board in a spot that doesn't obstruct the lobby might work, if approved. Outdoors, a weather-protected board could help, but its placement and cover would need approval too. It would be useful to check the actual spaces before choosing.
Can we just attach a temporary paper notice in the lobby for a week?

Ask whoever controls the lobby first, including whether temporary notices are allowed and where they can go. If they agree, a one-week trial could show whether residents notice it without committing to a permanent board.
Should I label my storage containers with handwritten tape or printed labels?
Handwritten tape is quick to change and needs little equipment. Printed labels can be easier to read consistently but take more setup. Are the contents likely to change often?
Some contain seasonal decorations; others change every month.
Try handwritten tape for the changing containers and printed labels for the seasonal ones. That gives you flexibility where you need it and a more consistent look for the stable contents.
I don't own a label printer.
Then handwritten tape may be the easiest starting point for all of them. If you already have access to a regular printer, paper labels under clear tape are another option, but they're not necessary.
I'm worried the handwriting won't be readable from a shelf.
Use a thick marker, large block letters, and short names. Test one container from your usual viewing distance before labeling the rest.
The tape peels off the textured bins.
Try a removable tag tied to a handle, if the bins have handles, or test a different removable label on one bin. Check that it stays attached and comes off cleanly before using it everywhere.
I want to plan a low-key celebration, but I'm torn between a surprise and involving the person.
What do they usually enjoy about celebrations, and do you know how they feel about surprises?
They like seeing close friends, but I don't know if they like surprises.
You could ask what kind of gathering they'd enjoy without revealing every detail. That lets them shape the event while leaving room for a small surprise, if they seem comfortable with one.
I don't want them to have to organize anything.
Ask for only a few preferences, such as whether they'd like a gathering, who they'd want there, and any dates to avoid. You can handle arrangements if they say yes.
They said dinner sounds nice, but only with three friends.
Plan around those three friends and the dinner they agreed to. For a surprise element, you might ask whether they'd enjoy a small surprise during the evening; their answer can guide you.
They said no surprises. One friend suggested inviting more people anyway.
Keep the guest list to the three friends they requested. You can tell the friend the plan is a small dinner and offer to include their help with something within that plan, if useful.
One of the three can't make that date.
Ask the person being celebrated whether they'd prefer another date or dinner with the two available friends. Either preserves their choice without assuming which matters more to them.
